doc.title: Manny Albam interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Learning from Georgie Auld's book, Budd Johnson and Dizzy
summary: He copied Auld's book and learned from Budd Johnson and Dizzy; he also mentions Van Alexander, Johnny Mandel and the Charles Colin studio.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: What was a chart going for back then?

Oh it wasn’t going for very much. Copying — I used to copy and Georgie, this is something that really taught me, you asked about books. I didn’t need books. I copied a lot of Georgie’s book. And the arrangers, one of the arrangers was Budd Johnson who © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

was a marvelous tenor player but he wrote a lot of stuff for Earl Hines’ band, Billy Eckstine’s band. And he would bring charts into my room, I had a great room on 52nd Street as a matter of fact. And when he gave me a new score I’d ask him about why he did certain things in the score that I was working on. And he would sit there for hours and tell me what Benny Carter told him and what this guy said about this, and why you put these notes together, it makes the thing ring a little bit more. He, and then later on Dizzy was another teacher I had, and there were no books anywhere. I can’t remember. Ultimately there was a book I think by Russ Garcia, but by then I think I knew all the stuff that was in there. And also Van Alexander’s book. I took a few lessons with Van. I couldn’t afford them, I couldn’t stay on. And at the time Johnny Mandel was studying with him and I was, and Johnny and I used to learn our instruments at the same place, at the Charles Colin studio. And there was a saxophone teacher that used to come in, and Johnny would learn trumpet at the time. He was a trumpet player to begin with and then he became a bass trumpet and trombone player. He studied with Charlie and I studied with Jay Arnold, who wrote a whole bunch of saxophone studies. And we hung out a lot together, John is a good old friend. And he really hit it with “I’m So Happy to See You.” He became very successful as you know.
